code.description: Source code to execute. Use console.log (JS/TS), print (Python/Ruby/Perl/R), echo (Shell), echo (PHP), fmt.Println (Go), IO.puts (Elixir), or Console.WriteLine (C#) to output a summary to context.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs (which is the right layer for this policy). Pass an explicit value for long-running builds (Gradle/Maven/SBT).

background.description: Keep process running after timeout (for servers/daemons). Returns partial output without killing the process. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add setTimeout/self-close timers in background scripts — the process must stay alive until the timeout detaches it. For server+fetch patterns, prefer putting both server and fetch in ONE ctx_execute call instead of using background.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for shell commands. Non-shell languages still execute from their sandbox temp directory.

intent.description:
What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), indexes output into knowledge base and returns section titles + previews — not full content. Use ctx_search(queries: [...]) to retrieve specific sections. Example: 'failing tests', 'HTTP 500 errors'.

TIP: Use specific technical terms, not just concepts. Check 'Searchable terms' in the response for available vocabulary.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file
entries.description:
Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. Running code over it here lets you keep the raw bytes out and only the derived answer in. Same principle as ctx_execute, scoped to one named file via the FILE_CONTENT variable.

WHEN:
  - You want to KNOW SOMETHING ABOUT a file (line count, matches of a pattern, parsed structure, statistical aggregate) without needing to SEE all of it
  - The file is structured (CSV, JSON, log, code) and a code-level derivation is cheaper than reading verbatim
  - The file is large enough that reading the full content would burn meaningful conversation memory you need for the actual work
  - The derivation may itself produce a large output you want recall-by-topic on later — pass an `intent` string; outputs over ~5KB are auto-indexed and only matching sections come back, retrievable via ctx_search

WHEN NOT:
  - You intend to EDIT the file — use Read so the subsequent Edit can match the exact text
  - You only need one specific line and you know its offset — Read with offset/limit is the simplest path
  - The file is small AND you will consume all of it for understanding/editing — Read directly

RETURNS:
  Only what your code prints. The FILE_CONTENT variable holds the raw bytes inside the sandbox; nothing else leaves. When `intent` is set and output exceeds the auto-index threshold, the response carries searchable section titles + previews instead of the raw stdout.

EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "huge.log", language: "javascript", code: "const errs = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n').filter(l => /ERROR|FATAL/.test(l)); console.log(`${errs.length} error lines`); console.log(errs.slice(-5).join('\\n'))")
EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "data.csv", language: "javascript", code: "const rows = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n'); console.log(`rows: ${rows.length - 1}, header: ${rows[0]}`)")

path.description: Absolute file path or relative to project root

code.description: Code to process FILE_CONTENT (file_content in Elixir). Print summary via console.log/print/echo/IO.puts/Console.WriteLine.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs.

intent.description: What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), returns only matching sections via BM25 search instead of truncated output.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-index call), then come back here to query
  - You have one ad-hoc question against data that is not in the knowledge base — answer it inline by running code in the sandbox tool; one round-trip instead of capture-then-query

RETURNS:
  Per-query ranked sections with window-extracted snippets. Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query. Common session-memory source labels: `decision` (user corrections / preferences), `error` and `error-resolution` (past failures + their fixes), `blocker`, `plan`, `user-prompt`, `rejected-approach`, `compaction` (post-compact session guide). See ctx_stats for live category counts. Each response carries a throttle counter (call #N/M in the rolling time window); results taper toward the soft cap and calls block after the hard cap. Tune via CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_WINDOW_MS, CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS_AFTER, CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_BLOCK_AFTER.

EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix", "test coverage"], source: "issue-#683")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["what did we decide about caching"], source: "decision", sort: "timeline")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["useEffect cleanup pattern"], source: "react-docs", contentType: "code", limit: 5)
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["last user prompt", "active skills", "open blockers"], sort: "timeline")

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

1	# Shim eraser: a dwell on the finished picture, then a quick wipe
2	
3	Issue #86. Written 2026-10-11 after talking it through with Rod.
4	
5	## Why
6	
7	xscreensaver hacks end a picture by calling `erase_window`. Upstream's
8	version waits, then wipes the picture away with an effect. Our shim clears
9	the window at once and returns NULL, so the order is reversed: the picture
10	goes, then the wait. Celtic waits 5 s (`delay2`) after the call. On the board
11	that 5 s is black, and the finished design never gets looked at.
12	
13	Rod saw Celtic on another device hold the design on screen and then wipe it.
14	That is the behaviour to bring back.
15	
16	## Goals
17	
18	- The first `erase_window` call draws nothing and returns a state, so a
19	  hack's wait happens with the finished picture still on screen.
20	- Later calls draw the next step of a wipe. The call after the wipe's end
21	  clears the window and returns NULL, as upstream does.
22	- A few cheap wipes, chosen at random, each about one second.
23	- No leak when a hack stops mid-wipe, for every hack, including the six
24	  that never call `eraser_free`.
25	
26	## Non-goals
27	
28	- Upstream's twelve effects, or its `eraseMode` and `eraseSeconds`
29	  resources.
30	- A look-alike of `utils/erase.c`. Shim code is ours: nothing is copied.
31	- Editing any copied hack. They stay byte-identical.
32	
33	## Anti-goals
34	
35	- A slow wipe. Rod's one wince: "a reeaeaallly slow wipe". Anything that
36	  takes visibly longer than about a second, or that drops the frame rate
37	  during the wipe, is a failure even if it is correct.
38	- A wipe that adds a full-frame push per step where a partial push would do.
39	
40	## What the callers do
41	
42	All eleven registered callers already follow upstream's contract: store the
43	return in `st->eraser`, call again while it is non-NULL, wait 10 to 33 ms
44	between steps. Read for this design:
45	
46	- Celtic, Coral, Critical, Epicycle, Helix, Maze, Pedal, Rorschach and
47	  XSpirograph call `erase_window` directly.
48	- `xlockmore.c` calls it for every xlockmore hack with `needs_clear`, waits
49	  33 ms while the state is live, and clears directly when nothing has been
50	  drawn yet.
51	- Only Pedal, Celtic, Epicycle and `xlockmore.c` call `eraser_free`.
52	  Coral, Rorschach, Critical, Maze, Helix and XSpirograph do not, so a
53	  stopped hack would leak a live state.
54	- Rorschach and Critical start drawing the next picture in the call that
55	  starts the erase. The first call draws nothing, so this is harmless
56	  there. A later step could wipe over fresh drawing, which is upstream's
57	  behaviour too.
58	
59	## Design
60	
61	### The state and the contract
62	
63	`erase_window(dpy, w, st)` in `x11shim/helpers.c` (or a new
64	`x11shim/erase.c`, the builder's choice) becomes a small state machine:
65	
66	- `st == NULL`: allocate a state, pick an effect at random, draw nothing,
67	  return the state. No start time yet.
68	- `st != NULL`, first step: record the start time now, draw ratio 0, return
69	  `st`.
70	- `st != NULL`, time left: draw the next step of the effect, return `st`.
71	- `st != NULL`, time up: finish with `XClearWindow`, free the state, return
72	  NULL.
73	
74	The start time is taken on the second call, not the first, because the dwell
75	sits between them. Celtic returns after the first call and is not called
76	again for `delay2` (5 s). A start time taken on the first call would find
77	the one-second wipe already over, and the picture would just vanish.
78	
79	`eraser_free(st)` frees the state and takes it off the display's list.
80	
81	### Progress comes from the clock, not the call count
82	
83	Each step computes its ratio from elapsed time over the duration. A caller
84	that steps every 10 ms and one that steps every 33 ms both finish in about
85	one second, and a slow frame cannot stretch the wipe. This is what keeps the
86	wipe from running slow on a busy board. The duration is one constant, about
87	one second.
88	
89	The shim's `double_time()` (`x11shim/doubletime.c`) reads the wall clock and
90	already has an override, `xshim_set_clock`. The host tests and the `dump`
91	program never sleep for a hack's returned delay, so on the wall clock a
92	wipe would not end inside a 3000-frame run, and pinned hashes would depend on
93	host speed. `test_hacks` already installs a fake clock through
94	`xshim_set_clock` that moves 1/30 s a reading, so the eraser reads
95	`double_time()` and is deterministic there. `dump` installs no clock, so it
96	gets the same fake one. This is my call, and it replaces my first idea of a
97	separate eraser clock hook, which the existing fake clock made unnecessary.
98	
99	### Effects
100	
101	Four, each a handful of fills in the window's background pixel:
102	
103	- Venetian blinds: bars grow from thin slats to solid.
104	- Circle wipe: a growing disc, centred on the window, clearing outward.
105	- Fizzle: a dissolve that fills random blocks until all are cleared.
106	- Random lines: lines in the background colour, thickening over time.
107	
108	The fill colour is the display's `window_background`, which
109	`XSetWindowBackground` sets and `XClearWindow` paints, so the wipe and the
110	final clear agree. The wipe fills the whole window and is not clipped to the
111	round panel (my call: the runner's corner clip already handles the push).
112	The canvas tracks dirty rows (`canvas_mark_dirty`), so the plan's first
113	check is that the fill calls used here mark them.
114	
115	Every step fills rectangles or lines rather than touching pixels one at a
116	time, so the cost is bounded by the number of fills, and rows dirtied stay
117	low where the effect allows. Venetian blinds and random lines dirty all
118	rows by their nature. This is acceptable for one second, and the push cost
119	is measured (see below) rather than assumed.
120	
121	### Cleanup for hacks that never free
122	
123	Live erasers are listed on the display. `runner.c`'s `stop()` releases them
124	after the hack's free callback, beside the existing `xshim_release_pixmaps`
125	call, which does the same for pixmaps ("as an X server does when a client
126	disconnects"). A hack that did call `eraser_free` has already removed its
127	state from the list, so there is no double free.
128	
129	This adds one line to the runner. It does not change what any hack sees, so
130	Rod's earlier go-ahead for the feature covers it.
131	
132	## Pinned frame hashes
133	
134	Any hack whose 200-frame test clears inside the window changes: Celtic's
135	picture finishes inside it. Each moved frame is looked at before the hash is

# Shim eraser: a dwell on the finished picture, then a quick wipe

Issue #86. Written 2026-10-11 after talking it through with Rod.

## Why

xscreensaver hacks end a picture by calling `erase_window`. Upstream's
version waits, then wipes the picture away with an effect. Our shim clears
the window at once and returns NULL, so the order is reversed: the picture
goes, then the wait. Celtic waits 5 s (`delay2`) after the call. On the board
that 5 s is black, and the finished design never gets looked at.

Rod saw Celtic on another device hold the design on screen and then wipe it.
That is the behaviour to bring back.

## Goals

- The first `erase_window` call draws nothing and returns a state, so a
  hack's wait happens with the finished picture still on screen.
- Later calls draw the next step of a wipe. The call after the wipe's end
  clears the window and returns NULL, as upstream does.
- A few cheap wipes, chosen at random, each about one second.
- No leak when a hack stops mid-wipe, for every hack, including the six
  that never call `eraser_free`.

## Non-goals

- Upstream's twelve effects, or its `eraseMode` and `eraseSeconds`
  resources.
- A look-alike of `utils/erase.c`. Shim code is ours: nothing is copied.
- Editing any copied hack. They stay byte-identical.

## Anti-goals

- A slow wipe. Rod's one wince: "a reeaeaallly slow wipe". Anything that
  takes visibly longer than about a second, or that drops the frame rate
  during the wipe, is a failure even if it is correct.
- A wipe that adds a full-frame push per step where a partial push would do.

## What the callers do

All eleven registered callers already follow upstream's contract: store the
return in `st->eraser`, call again while it is non-NULL, wait 10 to 33 ms
between steps. Read for this design:

- Celtic, Coral, Critical, Epicycle, Helix, Maze, Pedal, Rorschach and
  XSpirograph call `erase_window` directly.
- `xlockmore.c` calls it for every xlockmore hack with `needs_clear`, waits
  33 ms while the state is live, and clears directly when nothing has been
  drawn yet.
- Only Pedal, Celtic, Epicycle and `xlockmore.c` call `eraser_free`.
  Coral, Rorschach, Critical, Maze, Helix and XSpirograph do not, so a
  stopped hack would leak a live state.
- Rorschach and Critical start drawing the next picture in the call that
  starts the erase. The first call draws nothing, so this is harmless
  there. A later step could wipe over fresh drawing, which is upstream's
  behaviour too.

## Design

### The state and the contract

`erase_window(dpy, w, st)` in `x11shim/helpers.c` (or a new
`x11shim/erase.c`, the builder's choice) becomes a small state machine:

- `st == NULL`: allocate a state, pick an effect at random, draw nothing,
  return the state. No start time yet.
- `st != NULL`, first step: record the start time now, draw ratio 0, return
  `st`.
- `st != NULL`, time left: draw the next step of the effect, return `st`.
- `st != NULL`, time up: finish with `XClearWindow`, free the state, return
  NULL.

The start time is taken on the second call, not the first, because the dwell
sits between them. Celtic returns after the first call and is not called
again for `delay2` (5 s). A start time taken on the first call would find
the one-second wipe already over, and the picture would just vanish.

`eraser_free(st)` frees the state and takes it off the display's list.

### Progress comes from the clock, not the call count

Each step computes its ratio from elapsed time over the duration. A caller
that steps every 10 ms and one that steps every 33 ms both finish in about
one second, and a slow frame cannot stretch the wipe. This is what keeps the
wipe from running slow on a busy board. The duration is one constant, about
one second.

The shim's `double_time()` (`x11shim/doubletime.c`) reads the wall clock and
already has an override, `xshim_set_clock`. The host tests and the `dump`
program never sleep for a hack's returned delay, so on the wall clock a
wipe would not end inside a 3000-frame run, and pinned hashes would depend on
host speed. `test_hacks` already installs a fake clock through
`xshim_set_clock` that moves 1/30 s a reading, so the eraser reads
`double_time()` and is deterministic there. `dump` installs no clock, so it
gets the same fake one. This is my call, and it replaces my first idea of a
separate eraser clock hook, which the existing fake clock made unnecessary.

### Effects

Four, each a handful of fills in the window's background pixel:

- Venetian blinds: bars grow from thin slats to solid.
- Circle wipe: a growing disc, centred on the window, clearing outward.
- Fizzle: a dissolve that fills random blocks until all are cleared.
- Random lines: lines in the background colour, thickening over time.

The fill colour is the display's `window_background`, which
`XSetWindowBackground` sets and `XClearWindow` paints, so the wipe and the
final clear agree. The wipe fills the whole window and is not clipped to the
round panel (my call: the runner's corner clip already handles the push).
The canvas tracks dirty rows (`canvas_mark_dirty`), so the plan's first
check is that the fill calls used here mark them.

Every step fills rectangles or lines rather than touching pixels one at a
time, so the cost is bounded by the number of fills, and rows dirtied stay
low where the effect allows. Venetian blinds and random lines dirty all
rows by their nature. This is acceptable for one second, and the push cost
is measured (see below) rather than assumed.

### Cleanup for hacks that never free

Live erasers are listed on the display. `runner.c`'s `stop()` releases them
after the hack's free callback, beside the existing `xshim_release_pixmaps`
call, which does the same for pixmaps ("as an X server does when a client
disconnects"). A hack that did call `eraser_free` has already removed its
state from the list, so there is no double free.

This adds one line to the runner. It does not change what any hack sees, so
Rod's earlier go-ahead for the feature covers it.

## Pinned frame hashes

Any hack whose 200-frame test clears inside the window changes: Celtic's
picture finishes inside it. Each moved frame is looked at before the hash is
re-pinned, and Rod is asked before each re-pin. Per `AGENTS.md`, pin a hash
only from a build that is trusted by eye, after `srandom(1)`.

## Testing

- Host tests first (Unity, AddressSanitizer), clock injected.
- The first call draws nothing and returns non-NULL.
- Drawing between the first call and the end changes pixels, and the wipe
  ends with a fully cleared window and NULL.
- A step interval of 10 ms and one of 33 ms both end within a fixed
  tolerance of the duration. Mutation check: make progress count calls and
  watch this fail.
- Stopping mid-wipe through `runner_destroy` leaks nothing, for a hack that
  never calls `eraser_free` (compare
  `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()` at rest, as `test_hacks.c`
  does).
- Clip arithmetic uses `int64_t`. Assert pixels, not just survival: a clip
  bug on an inner row wraps unseen by AddressSanitizer.
- Mutation-check each new test: break the rule, watch it fail, then confirm
  with `git diff` that the change applied and was restored.

## Measuring on the board

The push cost of each effect has not been measured, and cannot be from the
host. Compile, host tests and a dump-frame check come first and are reported
separately from "runs on the device". Flashing needs Rod's explicit go-ahead
each time. When he gives it: flash a Celtic-pinned build, read the `run`
lines through a wipe, and report the lowest `fps=` window as well as the
mean. If any effect drops the frame rate or pushes more rows than it should,
drop that effect rather than slow the wipe.

## Left to the builder

- The file layout inside `x11shim/`.
- Exact effect parameters (slat count, fizzle block size, line widths).
- Which existing time source to use, and how to inject it for tests.
- Whether a fifth effect is worth adding. Not required.

## Decisions made without Rod

- Four effects, about one second, random pick (from the issue).
- Time-based progress, so a slow frame cannot stretch the wipe, started on
  the second call so the dwell is not counted.
- The eraser reads `double_time()`; `dump` gets the fake clock that
  `test_hacks` already uses.
- No clipping to the round panel.
- Cleanup through the display and the runner's `stop()`, because the six
  non-freeing hacks cannot be edited.

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` stops with "hypnowheel: does not compile ... 'rotator.h'
  file not found": a dropped GL port counts in the backtest and is probed
  standalone, without the GL helpers' include path. `docs/speed-backtest.md`
  was last regenerated before Hypnowheel was ported, and was not regenerated
  for the CWaves batch either. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is
  never compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as
  gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build
  without the After Dark disk (which lacks the toasters) still works.

  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
  overflow.
- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
  them when a hack stops.
- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse`, whose `double` maths is software on the S3. A
  test pins the pixels to `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  The older wrappers (Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame, Substrate) have not been
  checked.
- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); a bitmap or `None`
  draws nothing, and only `XCopyArea` writes into a bitmap (`XCopyPlane`
  follows the same rule). One exception still draws on the window whatever
  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
  ...)`. No
  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
  row. Without a
  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). The `logo_180`/`360`
  headers are aliases of the 50 px data, as a 466 px screen only picks 50.
  `XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repo root) swaps the logo for a local
  image, shrunk to fit 50 px, without committing it: `firmware/logo_override.py`
  writes the header into the build dir, where `maze_patched.c` finds it
  before the committed one. Unset, it deletes that header. Needs `uv`. A
  third-party logo kept under `vendor/` stays out of git that way. The WorkOS
  icon is `vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png`. A plain flash with it is
  `unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` then `XS_LOGO=vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png
  pio run -e stopwatch -t upload`: build flags stick, so a leftover pin from
  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.
- A wide circle through `XDrawArc` is a polyline of about a thousand wide
  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the
  polyline leaves gaps in it. `stroke_circle` (`x11shim/stroke.c`) fills the
  ring in two spans a row. Only Deluxe's wrapper calls it, and it does full
  circles only: Pacman's wall arcs are quarters and Celtic's wide strokes are
  lines, so they still take the stroker. Issue #56 asks whether the stroker's
  gaps and overpaint touch them. Changing shared stroke code can move their
  pinned frames: ask Rod.
- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the
  wide-line code in `stroke.c` blend over the canvas instead of overwriting it;
  fills, `canvas_line` and the other primitives ignore it. The canvas is
  byte-swapped RGB565, so the blend swaps each pixel and back. A shape of
  overlapping pieces (a polyline, a round cap and its segment) sets bits in a
  mask the size of the canvas (a 27 KB `calloc` per shape, freed at the end)
  and blends it once, or the overlaps blend twice and a star's corners show
  as bright diamonds. A failed `calloc` falls back to blending piece by piece.
  Setting `alpha` takes a wrapper, as in `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`.
- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
  pointer no mask is made.
- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
  (default 0), and `xshim_release_pixmaps` resets it when a hack stops: the
  display outlives the hack, and Hexadrop's colour once turned Pyro's clear
  into a solid fill. No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and draws every GC as
  `GXcopy`; it only remembers the function in `gc->function` now (GXcopy, GXor,
  GXxor). Halo and Moire2 handle both inside their own wrappers
  (`halo_planes.h`, `moire2_planes.h`).
- `screenhack.h`'s `frand` has a `1.0` inside its macro body, so the float
  literal pass cannot reach it and a single-precision wrapper still divides in
  double (software on the S3; `nm` shows `__divdf3`). `hacks/single_frand.h`
  redefines it in float; it is opt-in, because the older wrappers' frame hashes
  are pinned with the original.
- Added for the second batch, each test-first: 16-bit ZPixmap `XImage`s
  (canvas-order pixels, like every other value the shim hands out: `XAllocColor`
  -> `XPutPixel` -> `XPutImage` keeps the pixel; `XPutImage` does not swap.
  Only `lowrez_put_image` swaps, because Fireworkx writes ordinary RGB565
  bytes straight into the image data) and
  `ImageByteOrder`; `CoordModePrevious` in `XFillPolygon`, `XDrawLines` and
  `XDrawPoints`; `XCreatePixmapFromBitmapData` (X bitmap data is least
  significant bit first); a spline of our own (`spline.c`, not xscreensaver's);
  `XQueryColor`; `DisplayOfScreen` (the display opened last); the fill-rule,
  fill-style and stipple constants (accepted, ignored: fills are solid and
  even-odd); and `XSetFunction` and `jwxyz_XSetAlphaAllowed` (no-ops).
- Added for the third batch, each test-first: `ya_random` (the C library's
  `random()`, so `ya_rand_init` seeds it); `make_color_ramp` (the short way
  round the hue wheel, there and back when `closed_p`; ours, not
  xscreensaver's); `visual_depth` (always 16); `xshm.h` with
  `create_xshm_image`, `put_xshm_image` and `destroy_xshm_image`, which are a
  zeroed 16-bit `XImage` and `XPutImage` (`x11shim/xshm.c`); the arrow and page
  keysym constants (X's values; no key event ever arrives); and `glOrtho` (see
  `gl.md`). The Edit tool drops a trailing space from `old_string` and
  `new_string`: an edit that ends at a space in `platformio.ini`'s
  `build_src_filter` glued two entries together (it still built, which hid it).
- `allocate_alpha_colors` still finds no colour planes, so a hack that wants
  transparency (Qix, Goop) falls back to opaque layers and prints "couldn't
  allocate any color planes" on the host.
- The comment in `xshim.h` saying `XPutImage` byte-swaps a 16-bit image has
  been stale since commit 272ad6a: an `XImage` holds canvas-order pixels. A
  hack that builds its own 16-bit image must `px_swap` its pixels first.
